related_questions.question: Are RSV and respiratory infection the same thing?
related_questions.snippet: Respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, is a common respiratory virus that infects the nose, throat, and lungs. RSV symptoms make it difficult to distinguish it from the common cold or other respiratory viruses (like the flu or COVID-19). RSV spreads in the fall and winter along with other respiratory viruses.

related_questions.question: How long does RSV usually last?
related_questions.snippet: Most RSV infections go away on their own in a week or two. However, RSV can cause serious illness in some people.
related_questions.title: Symptoms and Care of RSV - CDC

related_questions.question: What are the first signs of RSV?
related_questions.snippet: People who become infected with RSV show symptoms within four to six days after the virus enter the body. Initial signs of RSV are similar to mild cold symptoms, including sneezing, runny nose, fever, cough and decrease in appetite. Very young infants may be irritable, fatigued and have breathing difficulties.
related_questions.title: RSV Symptoms and Diagnosis | American Lung Association

related_questions.question: What is the treatment for RSV?

text_blocks.snippet: Treatment for RSV (Respiratory Syncytial Virus) focuses on managing symptoms and supporting the body's natural healing process, as most cases resolve on their own within one to two weeks. For severe cases, especially in high-risk individuals like infants and those with underlying health conditions, hospitalization and more intensive treatments may be necessary.
snippet_highlighted_words: managing symptoms and supporting the body's natural healing process

text_blocks.snippet: Supportive Care (For Mild to Moderate Cases):

list.snippet: Fluids: Encouraging adequate fluid intake is crucial to prevent dehydration, especially in infants and children.
Fever and Pain Relief: Over-the-counter medications like acetaminophen or ibuprofen can help manage fever and discomfort. Aspirin should not be given to children.
Nasal Congestion: Saline drops and nasal suction can help clear mucus and relieve congestion.
Cool Mist Humidifier: A cool mist humidifier can help soothe irritated airways.
Rest: Adequate rest is important for recovery.

list.title: Difficulty Breathing:
list.snippet: Any signs of labored breathing, wheezing, or shortness of breath warrant immediate medical attention.

list.title: Dehydration:
list.snippet: Inability to drink enough fluids, leading to dehydration, requires medical intervention.

list.title: Worsening Symptoms:
list.snippet: If symptoms are not improving or are getting worse, consult a healthcare provider.

list.title: High-Risk Individuals:
list.snippet: Infants, young children with underlying health conditions (like chronic lung or heart problems), and older adults are at higher risk and should be closely monitored.
Oxygen Therapy: May be needed to ensure adequate oxygen levels in severe cases.
Bronchodilators: Inhalers or nebulizers may be used to open up airways, especially if there's evidence of bronchospasm (narrowing of the airways).
Intravenous Fluids: May be necessary to correct dehydration.
Antiviral Medications: Ribavirin, an antiviral medication, may be considered in very severe cases, but it has potential side effects and is typically reserved for high-risk individuals.
Mechanical Ventilation: In very severe cases, a ventilator may be needed to assist with breathing.
Nirsevimab: This is a monoclonal antibody that can provide protection against severe RSV illness in infants and young children.
Handwashing: Frequent handwashing with soap and water is crucial to prevent the spread of RSV.
Cover coughs and sneezes: Use a tissue or your elbow to cover your mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing.
Avoid close contact: If you are sick, avoid close contact with infants and young children.
Good Hygiene: Maintaining good hygiene practices can help prevent the spread of RSV.
